prose.text: The detection signals, the log fields and a carve-out for legitimate tunnels are open {{gap:tunnel-mechanics}}.

checks.do: Whether the rule's category selection includes the tunnels intended, since a parent category includes all of its tunnels.
Whether an answer presents detection signals or log fields as fact, since the captured pages do not state them.

tunnel-purpose.statement: DNS Control can detect and prevent DNS tunneling; Zscaler points to a separate page, Detecting and Controlling DNS Tunnels, for details.

quotes: DNS Control also allows you to detect and prevent DNS tunneling from occurring on your network. To learn more, see Detecting and Controlling DNS Tunnels.

tunnels-as-applications.statement: A DNS rule's `applications` field holds DNS tunnels and network applications.

quotes: DNS tunnels and network applications to which the rule applies

detection-method.statement: Detection uses machine learning: DNS proxy logs go to the analytics system and a detection engine that computes a risk score per domain; detected tunnel hostnames propagate to all ZIA Public Service Edges, and the proxy acts per your policy.

quotes: The detection engine uses advanced machine learning techniques to compute a risk score to classify domains.
When the engine detects a tunnel hostname, the information is propagated to all Public Service Edges for Internet & SaaS (ZIA).

three-categories.statement: Detected tunnels fall into three categories: Commonly Allowed (productive, mostly security services), Commonly Blocked (malicious or harmful) and Unknown (not yet classified); four further application categories (Network Service, Social Networking, Web, Web Search) can be controlled at DNS level.

quotes: Commonly Allowed DNS Tunnels: This contains tunnels that use DNS tunneling for productive reasons.
Unknown DNS Tunnels: This contains tunnels that are not yet classified.
There are 4 additional categories that you can control alongside the DNS tunnels:

logged-in-insights.statement: The service logs all detected DNS tunnels and network apps in DNS Insights, and the DNS Overview dashboard shows the most common ones.

quotes: The service logs all detected DNS tunnels and network apps in DNS Insights.

unknown-traffic-rule.statement: The predefined Unknown DNS Traffic rule, set to block, stops malformed queries and non-DNS traffic on port 53 and some forms of DNS abuse consistent with tunneling methods; Zscaler also recommends a rule blocking the Commonly Blocked and Unknown tunnel categories.

quotes: In addition, this rule also identifies and blocks certain forms of DNS abuse in real time that are consistent with certain DNS tunneling methods.

category-selection.statement: Selecting a parent tunnel category in a rule includes all tunnels in it.

quotes: selecting a parent category includes all of its members.

tunnel-mechanics.title: Detection signals, log fields, and a carve-out for legitimate tunnels
tunnel-mechanics.blocks: explaining why a query was or was not treated as a tunnel, and carving out legitimate tools
tunnel-mechanics.detail: Unverified legacy statement: Detection triggers on "anomalously long subdomain labels or query strings; high-entropy subdomain names; unusually high query rates for a single domain; DNS record types atypical for normal client usage (TXT, NULL, CNAME)"; matched queries are "logged with a tunnel-detection indicator"; "No separate 'allow tunnel' action exists"; and legitimate tools are carved out with "an Allow rule with explicit domain criteria above the tunnel-detection rule in order." The captured page says only that machine learning scores domains, so the signals are unconfirmed; the log is DNS Insights, with no named indicator field; the 'no allow action' wording conflicts with the Commonly Allowed category. Compare with a DNS log sample and a rule using the Commonly Allowed category.
